pack.description: Vocabulary of sociology passages and talks: social structure, groups, inequality and change.
pack.selection_note: Internal selection of terms that recur in introductory sociology texts; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: a way of behaving that a group of people considers normal and expected
entries.example_academic: Social norms are enforced less by law than by the disapproval of others.
entries.example_spoken: Tipping is the norm here, even for coffee.

entries.definition: the social or professional position of a person compared with others
entries.example_academic: Occupation remains one of the clearest markers of social status.
entries.example_spoken: He only bought that car for the status.

entries.definition: an unfair situation in which some people have more money, power or chances than others
entries.example_academic: Income inequality widened sharply during the last two decades of the century.
entries.example_spoken: There's a lot of inequality between the two neighborhoods.

entries.definition: relating to the size, age and other characteristics of a population
entries.example_academic: Demographic change has increased the proportion of people over sixty-five.
entries.example_spoken: The survey collects basic demographic information like age.

entries.definition: the process in which more and more people come to live in cities
entries.example_academic: Rapid urbanization placed enormous pressure on housing and sanitation.
entries.example_spoken: Urbanization has swallowed all the farmland around here.

entries.definition: a fixed and too simple idea about what a kind of person is like
entries.example_academic: Stereotypes persist partly because people notice the cases that confirm them.
entries.example_spoken: That's just a stereotype about engineering students.

entries.definition: to behave in the way that a group or rule expects
entries.example_academic: Participants conformed to the majority even when its answer was plainly wrong.
entries.example_spoken: He refuses to conform to what his family expects.

entries.definition: the process by which people, especially children, learn the values and behavior of their society
entries.example_academic: The family is the first agent of socialization, followed by school and peers.
entries.example_spoken: School isn't only about grades; it's about socialization too.

entries.definition: a system in which people or things are arranged in levels of importance
entries.example_academic: The hierarchy of the organization discouraged junior staff from voicing concerns.
entries.example_spoken: There's a clear hierarchy in that lab, and the professor is at the top.

entries.definition: to treat a person or group as unimportant and keep them away from power or attention
entries.example_academic: Policies that marginalize minority languages tend to accelerate their decline.
entries.example_spoken: Part-time students often feel marginalized on campus.

entries.definition: the state in which the members of a group stay united and support each other
entries.example_academic: Shared rituals strengthen social cohesion within a community.
entries.example_spoken: The team has no cohesion; everyone works alone.

entries.definition: a person of the same age, position or ability as another person
entries.example_academic: Adolescents are more strongly influenced by their peers than by their parents.
entries.example_spoken: She's much more mature than her peers.

entries.definition: the practice of treating a person or group worse than others for unfair reasons
entries.example_academic: The law prohibits discrimination in hiring on the basis of age.
entries.example_spoken: He filed a complaint about discrimination at work.

entries.definition: the policy or practice of keeping different groups of people apart
entries.example_academic: Residential segregation limits access to well-funded schools.
entries.example_spoken: The city still shows the effects of decades of segregation.

entries.definition: help, especially money, that a government gives to people in need; or a person's health and happiness
entries.example_academic: Critics argued that the welfare system discouraged people from seeking work.
entries.example_spoken: The university has an office for student welfare.

entries.definition: all the people who live together in one home
entries.example_academic: The average household now contains fewer than three people.
entries.example_spoken: Every household on the street got the same letter.

entries.definition: the division of a society into levels based on wealth, power or status
entries.example_academic: Social stratification determines access to education long before children enter school.
entries.example_spoken: The lecture on stratification was basically about class.

entries.definition: behavior that breaks the accepted rules of a society
entries.example_academic: What counts as deviance changes from one period to another.
entries.example_spoken: Tattoos used to be seen as deviance; now nobody cares.

entries.definition: strong control or leading influence of one group or country over others
entries.example_academic: Cultural hegemony operates by making the dominant group's values appear natural.
entries.example_spoken: English has a kind of hegemony in science publishing.

entries.definition: a system in which people gain power or success because of their ability and not their background
entries.example_academic: The belief in meritocracy can hide the advantages that some children inherit.
entries.example_spoken: They call it a meritocracy, but connections still matter.

entries.definition: the process in which richer people move into a poor area and change it, so that the original residents can no longer afford to stay
entries.example_academic: Gentrification raised property values but displaced long-term tenants.
entries.example_spoken: My old neighborhood is unrecognizable after all the gentrification.

entries.definition: to treat a person or group as if they should feel ashamed
entries.example_academic: Societies that stigmatize mental illness discourage people from seeking treatment.
entries.example_spoken: Nobody should be stigmatized for asking for help.

entries.definition: the networks of relationships and trust that help people and groups achieve things
entries.example_academic: Communities rich in social capital recover more quickly from natural disasters.
entries.example_spoken: Joining clubs is a good way to build social capital.

entries.definition: the process by which religion loses influence over society and public life
entries.example_academic: Secularization proceeded more slowly in rural regions than in industrial cities.
entries.example_spoken: The professor linked falling church attendance to secularization.

entries.definition: a group of people who share a feature, especially being born or starting something in the same period
entries.example_academic: The study followed a cohort of children born in the same year.
entries.example_spoken: Everyone in my cohort is graduating in June.

entries.definition: based on the belief that all people should have the same rights and chances
entries.example_academic: Hunter-gatherer bands are often described as broadly egalitarian.
entries.example_spoken: Our seminar is pretty egalitarian; everyone gets to speak.

entries.definition: the process by which a person or group becomes part of a larger society and takes on its ways
entries.example_academic: Assimilation was expected of immigrants, who were urged to abandon their languages.
entries.example_spoken: My grandparents talked a lot about the pressure of assimilation.

entries.definition: to take away the right to vote or other power from a person or group
entries.translation_fr: priver du droit de vote, priver de ses droits
entries.example_academic: Literacy tests were used to disenfranchise large sections of the population.
entries.example_spoken: Young voters feel disenfranchised by the new rules.

entries.definition: movement to a higher social or economic position
entries.example_academic: Access to university has long been regarded as the main route to upward mobility.
entries.example_spoken: For my parents, a degree meant upward mobility.
